newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian imports show some life in economy.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian imports show some life in economy.

text.p: Australia's import bill rose for the fifth successive month in December, a sign that the economy may having been grathered some pace into the end of 1996, analysts said on Monday.
However, despite the encouraging signs, an interest rate cut in the next couple of months was still on the cards, they said.
Merchandise imports rose by 0.8 percent in the month, after rises of around one percent in each of the previous four months, the official data showed.
"The pace of import demand is consistent with a moderate and steady pace of domestic demand growth," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.
Imports are one indicator of demand in the economy, and the recent run of rises has suggested that there may be some preliminary signs of an uptick in activity.
"There is life in the economy yet," Colonial State Bank chief economists Hans Kunnen said, "and maybe more life than we had been prepared to admit."

However, the breakdown of the imports rise was not seen as the most favourable mix. Within the total rise, consumer goods were up 1.5 percent, intermediate goods were up 3.8 percent, while capital goods fell 6.3 percent.
Capital goods are seen as an indicator of business investment, and the fact that they have fallen 7.7 percent over the December quarter caused some concern.
If capital good imports remained weak, it might raise some questions over whether the government's growth forecasts would be met, economists said.
Westpac senior economist John Peters said capital goods weakness "reflecting waning business confidence and investment activity on the back of weakening domestic activity over 1996."

Some of the strength in imports was attributable to the rise in the Australian dollar through 1996, making imports more competitive. Economists said that the fall in import costs over the past year due to the stronger dollar might now be leading to a lift in import volumes.
Commonwealth Bank economist Michael Blythe said rough calculations showed import volumes had risen around five percent in the December quarter.
"This is consistent with an economy that, while subdued overall, retains some momentum," Blythe said.
However, the momentum was not sufficient to definitively rule out another interest rate cut, he said, a sentiment with which others agreed.
At Westpac, Peters said the data was consistent with flat domestic demand over late 1996, and "is consistent with our view that another rate cut is warranted to revive a still flat economy."

The rate cut case would be bolstered by what economists expect will be favourable December quarter inflation data, due next week, and a reaffirmation if the government's commitment to return its budget to balance when the mid-year review is released.

The mid-year review, expected before the end of Janaury, may also contain some downward revisions to economic forecasts, such as employment, which would see expectations of a rate cut build, economists said.
